findings.title: thread.join(timeout=...) can expire while a heartbeat write is in flight, letting a stale RUNNING write land after the caller's terminal DONE/FAILED write
findings.detail: _heartbeat's finally block only signals the daemon thread and joins it with a bounded timeout (heartbeat_seconds() + 5, i.e. 6-65s depending on NGIAB_JOB_STALE_SECONDS). The loop body (lines 249-252) has no cooperative cancellation check between snapshot() and write_status(): once a tick has passed stop.wait() and entered the body, it will complete its write_status() call regardless of stop having been set concurrently. Ordering after a normal (non-timing-out) join is guaranteed because publish() does not return, and the command does not write its terminal status, until join() returns. But if write_status()/_replace() is slow enough (network stall talking to S3, contended local disk, etc.) to exceed the join timeout, join() returns anyway (silently -- no exception, no log message) while the beat thread's write_status call is still in progress. publish() then returns, the command's ingest_archive.handle() writes the terminal DONE (or _fail writes FAILED) status, and if the stalled beat write completes afterward it clobbers that terminal document with {state: RUNNING, stage: <stale stage>, message: <stale message>} and no 'run' key. This directly reintroduces the class of bug the commit sets out to fix: the client (ngiab-upload-run.js) sees terminal=false again and keeps polling a job that has already finished/failed, until POLL_CEILING_MS eventually gives up with a misleading 'taking longer than expected' message even though the run was already published (or already failed) on disk/storage.
findings.why_it_matters: The docstring for _heartbeat explicitly claims 'The thread is joined rather than merely signalled ... a beat already in flight has to land before the caller writes its terminal status, or it would put RUNNING back over DONE' -- but the join has a timeout and nothing detects or logs when it is exceeded, so the documented invariant silently fails to hold under slow storage. This is exactly the ordering hazard the review brief called out ('thread.join(timeout=...) can time out. What then?').
findings.reproduction_sketch: Monkeypatch write_status (or the storage backend's save/path) to block for longer than heartbeat_seconds()+5 seconds while a beat is executing it, then let publish() return and have the caller write a terminal status; assert the terminal status survives -- it does not once the delayed beat write finally completes.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) do not let the beat write unconditionally -- have it check `stop.is_set()` again immediately before calling write_status and/or pass a monotonically increasing generation/token so a write started before stop can be recognized as stale and discarded by the writer instead of the caller, or (b) make write_status conditional: read the current status first and skip/log if it is already terminal (compare-and-write), so a late heartbeat can never regress a terminal state regardless of the join timeout. At minimum, log a warning when thread.join() times out so this failure mode is observable instead of silent.

residual_risks.title: Heartbeat writes omit the 'run' field that stage-transition writes include
residual_risks.detail: write_status replaces the whole payload each time it is called (payload = {job, updated, **fields}); the beat calls it with only state/stage/message (ingest.py line 252), never 'run'. Currently harmless because the only consumer of status.run in the frontend (ngiab-upload-run.js lines 165/171) reads it solely once status.terminal is true, and every terminal write (DONE/FAILED in ingest_archive.py's handle()/_fail()) always supplies run= explicitly, so the field is present exactly when it is read. But this is fragile: any future non-terminal consumer of status.run (e.g. a status/admin view added later, or a UI that shows the target run name while 'converting…') would see it intermittently disappear for the length of a heartbeat tick every time a beat fires between two real stage writes.

residual_risks.title: Torn read of the mutable `at` snapshot dict is theoretically possible
residual_risks.detail: say() does at.update(stage=stage, message=message) as two separate dict item assignments on the main thread while the heartbeat thread concurrently reads at['stage'] and at['message'] without a lock. Under the GIL each individual assignment/read is atomic, but the pair is not, so a heartbeat tick could in principle observe a new stage paired with the previous message (or vice versa) for one write. Purely cosmetic (a status message momentarily describing the wrong stage) and self-corrects on the next write; not flagged as a finding.

testing_gaps: No test exercises thread.join() actually timing out (e.g. by making write_status/backend.save block past heartbeat_seconds()+5) to verify what happens to a terminal status written immediately afterward.
No test asserts that 'run' survives being read while a heartbeat is actively ticking mid-stage (only checked at/after DONE, where the command's own write re-supplies it).

No test covers _replace()/write_status() concurrency: the beat thread and the main thread (via progress()/say()) can call write_status() for the same job_id at nearly the same time; there's no test pinning that the two independent temp-file+os.replace sequences don't produce a visible regression in 'updated' ordering under contention.
